Hennepin Cty. Dist. Ct., Minn. · No. 27‑CR‑20‑12646 · D. Minn. · No. 0:21‑cr‑00108 State v. Chauvin George Floyd died on May 25, 2020, after Minneapolis police officers held him face down on the street, handcuffed, for about nine and a half minutes, one of them, Derek Chauvin, with a knee on his neck. The State of Minnesota charged Chauvin with murder, and in April 2021, after a trial televised from start to finish, a jury found him guilty. He was sentenced to 22 and a half years. He then pleaded guilty in federal court to violating Floyd’s civil rights, and is serving 21 years for that at the same time. His appeals have failed, but he’s still challenging both convictions, and three of those challenges are still open. Charged May 29, 2020 Before Cahill, J. · Magnuson, J. Verdict Apr 20, 2021 Status Convicted

Prosecution The side bringing the charges Through the state Attorney General The case is brought in the name of the State of Minnesota. The Hennepin County Attorney filed the first charges on May 29, 2020, and two days later Gov. Tim Walz put the state’s Attorney General, Keith Ellison, in charge of the prosecution. Four of its lawyers sat in court at a time: two assistant attorneys general, Matthew Frank and Erin Eldridge, and two outside lawyers who worked for free, Jerry Blackwell and Steve Schleicher. Ellison came for the sentencing. On appeal the State was represented by Neal Katyal. In the federal case the prosecution was the United States. Complaint, May 29, 2020 · WCCO, May 31, 2020 · AP, Apr 4, 2021 · Sentencing order p. 1 · Ct. App. opinion p. 1

Defendant The person charged Minneapolis police officer at the time Born in 1976, he had been a Minneapolis police officer for more than 18 years by May 2020. He also trained new officers on the street, and was training one the day of the 2017 arrest he later admitted using excessive force in. Eric Nelson defended him at trial and in the federal case, paid through a statewide police association’s legal defense fund. William Mohrman took his appeal. Since 2024 a federal public defender has handled his motion to undo his plea, and Gregory Joseph his petitions in state court. He’s in federal prison in Texas, serving both sentences at once. How this was made, and what it leaves out

Built from the record the trial court posts for this case: the complaints, the judge’s orders, the jury instructions, the verdict forms, the sentencing order, and the briefs on appeal. Then the Court of Appeals’ 2023 opinion, the U.S. Supreme Court’s docket, and the federal case’s filings, read through the archive of federal court records on CourtListener. Each side is described in its own words in court or in its own filings. The trial itself was never posted as a court reporter’s transcript, so words spoken in the courtroom are quoted from transcripts of the broadcast and cited by its clock. The court’s website sometimes refuses a request it takes for a robot, and a browser gets through. Minnesota Judicial Branch, case page · Federal docket · Ct. App. opinion

His petitions since 2024, the State’s answers to them, and the trial court’s orders on them aren’t on the court’s case page. The parts of these pages about them rest on news reports, and each one is cited. Neither are the trial exhibits. The results of the tissue testing in the federal case haven’t been made public. The jurors’ names were released by the court in November 2021. These pages don’t use them. Jurors are known here by number, as they were in court. Order of Oct 25, 2021 p. 3 · Star Tribune, Dec 4, 2025 · MPR News, Aug 18, 2026

There are five numbers for how long he was held down, and each one belongs to someone. The first complaint said his knee was on Floyd’s neck for 8 minutes and 46 seconds. The judge’s 2020 order said “more than nine minutes and twenty seconds.” At trial the State said 9 minutes and 29 seconds, and the appeals court used that. The judge’s sentencing findings said “more than nine minutes and forty seconds,” and his federal plea says about ten minutes. These pages say whose number they use. People are named when they’re a party, a lawyer, a judge, or a witness who testified in public. The young witnesses aren’t named, except Darnella Frazier, whose video and testimony are public under her own name. The 14-year-old in the 2017 case isn’t named, as the federal record doesn’t name him. Amended complaint p. 4 · Order of Oct 21, 2020 p. 29 · Ct. Not legal advice, not a finding, and not a verdict. He stands convicted of second-degree murder in state court and of violating Floyd’s civil rights in federal court. What he argues in his petitions is reported here as his argument, and the courts haven’t accepted any of it so far. The other three officers were tried, or pleaded, in cases of their own. These pages mention them only where they’re part of his. Where the record doesn’t reach, these pages say so and stop. AP, Feb 24, 2022
The state trial court for Minneapolis and the county around it. Judge Peter Cahill tried the case there. A different judge, Paul Scoggin, has heard his petitions since.
The state court that hears appeals from trial courts. Three of its judges decide each case.
The state’s highest court. It chooses which appeals to hear, and it turned down his.
The United States’ own courts, separate from the state’s. The federal case was in the U.S. District Court in St. Paul, before Judge Paul Magnuson.
Minnesota’s chief lawyer, elected statewide. Keith Ellison’s office took over the prosecution from the county prosecutor in May 2020.
A state and the federal government count as separate governments, so each can prosecute the same act under its own laws. That isn’t double jeopardy.
The document that starts a criminal case in Minnesota. It lists the charges and the facts the prosecutor says support them. An amended complaint replaces it.

A group of citizens who hear the prosecutor’s evidence in private and decide whether to charge someone. Minnesota only requires one for crimes that carry life in prison, like first-degree murder, so this case started with a complaint instead.
A charge brought by a grand jury. The federal case started with one.
A charge a prosecutor files without a grand jury. In federal court that takes the defendant’s consent, which he gave for the 2017 count.
The court’s numbered list of everything filed in a case. Entry 42 is the forty-second thing filed.
A written deal between a defendant and the prosecutors. He pleads guilty to some charges, and they agree on others to drop and on a range of sentence.
A word-for-word record. The court reporter’s transcript of this trial was never posted, so these pages quote transcripts typed from the court’s own video feed and cite them by its clock.
Causing a death, without meaning to, while committing a felony. Here the felony was third-degree assault. This is the one count he was convicted and sentenced on.
Intentionally using unlawful force on someone, without their consent, that causes substantial bodily harm. He only had to mean to use the force, not to cause that much harm.
Causing a death by an act “eminently dangerous” to others, done with “a depraved mind,” without meaning to kill. Also called depraved-mind murder.
Causing a death by culpable negligence, which means consciously taking a chance of causing death or great harm that an ordinary careful person would see.
A crime contained in a more serious one. Minnesota law allows only one conviction for the same act, so the other two guilty verdicts were never entered as convictions.
Acting with the power of a government job, like a police officer on duty. The federal civil rights law makes it a crime to use that power to take away someone’s constitutional rights.
Intentionally helping someone else commit a crime. The other three officers were charged that way.
Enough evidence to make it reasonable to believe a person committed the crime. It’s the bar a charge has to clear to go to trial, and it’s a lot lower than proof.
Where a trial is held. A defendant can ask to move it if publicity would make a fair jury impossible where the crime happened.
Putting a trial or a hearing off to a later date.
Splitting one trial of several defendants into separate trials.
Keeping jurors away from news and the public, sometimes in a hotel, so nothing outside the courtroom reaches them.
Questioning possible jurors one by one to find out if they can be fair. Also called voir dire.
Removing a possible juror without giving a reason. Each side gets a set number. Here the judge raised his to 18 and the State’s to 10.
Removing a possible juror for a specific reason they can’t be fair, like having already made up their mind. There’s no limit on these.
A juror who hears the whole trial but only deliberates if one of the twelve has to leave.
Jurors known in court only by number, their names kept from the public until the judge releases them.
Evidence of something that happened before the case, which a jury may only use for a narrow purpose the judge sets. Minnesota calls it Spreigl evidence.
The right not to be a witness against yourself. A defendant who uses it doesn’t testify, and the jury is told it can’t hold that against him.
Evidence or argument that answers the other side’s. The State goes last because it has to prove the case.
The level of proof needed to convict. It means proof that leaves the jury firmly convinced, not proof beyond every possible doubt.
All twelve jurors agreeing. A verdict in a criminal case has to be.
Asking each juror out loud, one at a time, if the verdict read is theirs.
The test for causing a death. His acts didn’t have to be the only cause, only a substantial one. Other causes don’t excuse him unless one of them alone caused the death.
Something that comes afterward and breaks the chain, so that it alone causes the death. It’s the one way another cause can clear a defendant.
The defense the jury was told about. No crime is committed if a police officer uses reasonable force to make a lawful arrest, and the State had to prove his force wasn’t that.
How force is judged. The question is what a reasonable officer in the same situation would have done at the moment the force was used, not what the officer meant or what hindsight shows.
Holding a person face down. Police training warns it can make it hard to breathe, and says to move the person onto their side once they’re under control.
Rolling a person onto their side so they can breathe more easily. The Minneapolis police’s own training said to do it.
A strap that ties a person’s legs together. The officers talked about using one and didn’t.

The Minneapolis police method of strapping a struggling person’s legs and moving them off their stomach. The defense said what the officers did began as one. The State said the knee was no part of it.
Death from not getting enough oxygen. The State’s doctors said the restraint caused it.
A rare tumor that can release adrenaline. One was found at the autopsy and called incidental, meaning the medical examiner didn’t think it played a part.
Minnesota’s chart of how long a sentence should be for each crime, set by a state commission. A judge has to stay inside its range unless there are substantial and compelling reasons not to.
What the guidelines call for. For this crime and no past record it’s 150 months, inside a range of 128 to 180.
A fact that makes a crime worse than the usual one of its kind, like particular cruelty. It has to be proved before a judge can go past the guidelines.
A 2004 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that a jury has to find the facts behind a longer sentence, unless the defendant gives that up. He gave it up, so the judge decided them.
A sentence longer than the guidelines’ range. His was 270 months against a top of 180.
Served at the same time. His state and federal sentences run together, not one after the other.
A period after a federal prison term when a person lives under conditions the court sets, checked by a probation officer.
Asking the trial judge to throw out the verdict and start over because something went wrong. It comes before any appeal.
A hearing in Minnesota where a judge questions jurors about possible misconduct after a trial. He asked for one and was refused.
The first appeal after a conviction, which looks only at what happened at trial. His was decided in 2023.
Asking the Minnesota Supreme Court to hear a case after the Court of Appeals has ruled. It turns most of them down.
Asking the U.S. Supreme Court to hear a case. It takes very few, and turning one down decides nothing about the case itself.
A way to challenge a state conviction after the appeal is over, usually with something that wasn’t in the trial record. It goes back to the trial court first.
Minnesota’s rule that a petition after the appeal can’t raise what was raised, or could have been raised, on appeal, with narrow exceptions.
A mistake in how a case was run that’s so basic a court doesn’t ask whether it changed the result. His lawyer says the way he was charged is one.
The federal version of a post-conviction petition, under section 2255 of the federal code. His asks to undo his federal guilty plea.
A lawyer’s work falling so far short that it denied the client a fair process. It’s the one kind of claim his plea deal let him bring later.
Pausing a case, or a ruling, until something else is decided.
The court said yes to the request on this card, whichever side made it.
The court gave some of what was asked for on this card and said no to the rest.
The court said no to the request on this card.
A charge that had been dismissed was put back, so the jury could decide it.
The jury’s verdict, or his own plea in court. It becomes a conviction once the court enters judgment on it.
The court above agreed with the court below and left the conviction and the sentence as they were.
Thrown out without a ruling on whether the claims in it were right.

Where it stands Both convictions stand, and three challenges are open. In the state courts, his appeal of the May 2026 denial and a third petition filed in August 2026. In federal court, his motion to undo his guilty plea, on hold since January 2025 while Floyd’s tissue is tested. The state case State of Minnesota v. Chauvin, in Hennepin County, for murder. Did the State prove he committed a crime?

Three charges, one evening Yes · guilty on all three, Apr 20, 2021 This is the trial. The State charged him with three crimes for the same nine and a half minutes, and to convict on any of them the jury had to be sure of every piece beyond a reasonable doubt. Twelve people had to agree, which is what unanimous means, and they had to look at each charge separately. Two of the pieces are the same for all three charges, so they sit first inside this card. The third is what makes each charge different. All three are needed, so a no on any one of them for a charge means not guilty on that charge. Who must prove it The State. He didn’t have to prove anything, and he didn’t testify. All three are needed and and
Did his actions cause George Floyd’s death?

Yes · the jury found it This was the biggest fight in the trial. The jury was told his actions didn’t have to be the only cause, just a substantial causal factor. So heart disease or drugs playing a part wouldn’t clear him, unless one of them alone caused the death, which the law calls a superseding cause. The State’s doctors said Floyd died of a lack of oxygen from being held face down with a knee on his neck. The defense’s medical examiner said his heart gave out, with drugs and other things adding to it. The jury went with the State.
Was his force more than a reasonable officer would use?

Yes · the jury found it Police are allowed to use force to arrest someone, so the jury was told no crime is committed if an officer uses reasonable force making a lawful arrest. That’s the authorized use of force, and the State had to prove his wasn’t. It’s judged the way a reasonable officer would see it at that moment, not with hindsight. The State said any force had to end once Floyd was handcuffed, face down and not resisting. The defense said you have to count the whole struggle before that and the angry crowd.
Does what he did fit each of the three crimes?

Yes · on all three Each charge needs something more, and none of them needs an intent to kill. Second-degree unintentional murder means he caused the death while committing a felony, here third-degree assault, which means meaning to use the force and the force causing serious harm. Third-degree murder means an act “eminently dangerous” to others with no regard for life. Second-degree manslaughter means consciously taking a big risk that an ordinary careful person would see. The jury said guilty on all three.

Outcome Then He walks out of court If the jury had a reasonable doubt about the cause or the force, that’s not guilty on every charge, and the State can’t appeal an acquittal. A doubt about one charge’s own piece would only clear him of that charge. That isn’t what happened. The jury agreed on all three by early afternoon on its second day.
Should his sentence go past the guidelines?

Only one conviction, the most serious Yes · 270 months, Jun 25, 2021 Guilty on three charges doesn’t mean three sentences. Minnesota only lets the court convict on the most serious one for the same act, so he was convicted of second-degree murder, and the other two verdicts were never entered. The state’s sentencing guidelines say that for him, with no record, the sentence should be 150 months, between 128 and 180. To go higher the judge needs an aggravating factor, something that makes this crime worse than the usual one. He gave up his right to have a jury decide those facts, which a ruling called Blakely gives him, so the judge did, and found four. He leaned on two, the particular cruelty and the abuse of his authority as an officer, and gave him 270 months, which is 22 and a half years. That’s an upward departure. Either way, the case would go on to an appeal. What each side asked The State asked for 30 years. He asked for probation.

Twelve claims, decided together No · affirmed Apr 17, 2023 After a conviction comes the direct appeal, where a higher court looks for mistakes in the trial. It doesn’t hear new evidence or decide again whether he did it. His lawyer gave the Court of Appeals twelve reasons, and these are the three that mattered most. Any one of them could have gotten him a new trial, so a yes on any one was enough. The court said no to all twelve, the sentence included. The Minnesota Supreme Court and the U.S. Supreme Court both refused to take the case after that, which ended it. A yes on any one is enough or or
Should the trial have been moved, delayed or the jury locked away?

No · the jury was shown to be fair He said nobody in Minneapolis could judge him fairly, after the riots, the city’s $27 million settlement in the middle of jury selection, the courthouse wrapped in razor wire and soldiers, and a congresswoman telling protesters to get more confrontational. The court said publicity this big was going to follow the case anywhere, and what counts is whether the judge did enough to get a fair jury anyway. It said he did, with questionnaires, jurors questioned one at a time, extra strikes for the defense and jurors removed for cause.
Did a juror hide views that should have kept him off?

No · his answers were true After the verdict, Juror 52 told a radio interviewer he’d been pulled over by Minneapolis police “probably about 50 times,” and it came out that he’d gone to a march in Washington in August 2020 where Floyd’s family spoke. Chauvin said he hid that in jury selection and asked for a hearing to question him. The court said his answers on the questionnaire were true as written, and Chauvin had three strikes left he could have used.
Is it wrong to convict an officer of felony murder for force in an arrest?

No · he can be convicted This one was about the law itself. Felony murder here rests on assault, and he said officers have to use force to arrest people, so the charge basically turns every officer into a criminal whenever someone dies. The court said no. Officers are only allowed reasonable force, so force that’s unreasonable can be an assault like anyone else’s. That ruling is now the law in Minnesota.

Outcome Then Maybe somewhere else The conviction would be thrown out and the State could try him again, maybe in another county. Not every mistake gets that. A court has to think it could have changed the result. None of the claims got that far.
Is there a reason to reopen the case now?

The case is here After the appeal is over Undecided Once the appeals are done, a post-conviction petition is the last way back into a state court. It usually needs something the trial record didn’t have. And under the Knaffla rule, it can’t just argue again what was argued on appeal, or could have been. He’s filed three since 2024 with his new lawyer, Gregory Joseph. The first was dismissed in 2025. The other two are open, and they argue different things, so they’re the two cards inside this one. A yes on either would reopen the case. A yes on either one is enough or
Did the trial rest on wrong testimony or wrong instructions?

No · denied May 1, 2026 · appealed This one says the State’s doctors drew their conclusions from video instead of medical findings, that the police chief and two trainers misdescribed what the department taught, backed by statements from 57 officers, and that the jury instructions were flawed. Judge Paul Scoggin said none of it warranted relief, and that most of it was or could have been argued on appeal. Chauvin appealed in June 2026, and the Court of Appeals hasn’t ruled.
Was he charged the wrong way from the start?

Undecided This one isn’t about the evidence. It says the governor had no right to hand the case to the Attorney General, and that charging him without a grand jury let prosecutors decide on their own what a grand jury should have. He calls that a structural error, so basic that the whole case would have to go. He’s asked the Court of Appeals to pause his other appeal so the trial court can hear this one first. No ruling had been reported by October 22, 2026.

Outcome Then He keeps serving his sentence If every petition fails, the conviction and the 270 months stay as they are, and the State never has to try him again. He’s serving the state sentence at the same time as the federal one, in federal prison.

Outcome Then A new trial, or the charges thrown out The second petition asks for a new trial or at least a hearing. The third asks for much more, that the conviction be vacated and the charges dismissed. Even then his federal conviction, which he pleaded guilty to, wouldn’t be touched by anything a state court does.
Did he violate George Floyd’s constitutional rights?
United States v. Chauvin · St. Paul

Decided by his own plea Yes · his plea, Dec 15, 2021 This is a different crime in a different court. The federal law makes it a crime for someone using the power of a government job, under color of law, to take away a person’s rights, here the right to be free from unreasonable force by police. It doesn’t matter that the state already convicted him, because the state and the federal government are separate governments with their own laws. There was no jury question here, because he answered it himself. He pleaded guilty, and admitted his force “became objectively unreasonable and excessive” once the officers decided not to tie Floyd’s legs. He also pleaded guilty over the 2017 arrest of a 14-year-old. The judge gave him 21 years, running at the same time as the state sentence. His plea deal Gave up most appeals and most later challenges, except a claim that his lawyer failed him.
Should his guilty plea be undone?

The case is here The one challenge his deal allowed Undecided He says his lawyer, Eric Nelson, never told him that a pathologist had written to Nelson and the judge during the state trial with a theory that a rare tumor found at the autopsy, a paraganglioma, caused Floyd’s death. If he’d known, he says, he wouldn’t have pleaded guilty. That’s a claim of ineffective assistance, and to win it he needs both cards inside this one. The judge let his experts examine Floyd’s heart tissue in December 2024 and put the hearing on hold for the testing in January 2025. Nothing public has happened since. Both are needed and
Did his lawyer fall short by not telling him?

Undecided The question isn’t whether the tumor theory is right. It’s whether a reasonable lawyer would have told his client about it before he pleaded. The government says it wouldn’t have mattered anyway, because the autopsy findings came out at the state trial and the jury wasn’t persuaded by the same kind of argument.
Would he have gone to trial if he’d known?

Undecided He also has to show a real chance he’d have turned the deal down and gone to trial. He says he would have. At his plea hearing he told the judge he understood what he was giving up, and in his plea agreement he admitted that his actions kept Floyd from getting enough oxygen to live.

Outcome Then 21 years, at the same time as the state sentence The federal conviction and sentence stay as they are, and his deal leaves him almost nothing else to bring. His state conviction is a separate question, for the state courts.

Outcome Then Back to the start of the federal case Undoing the plea wouldn’t clear him. It would put the federal charges back where they were before he pleaded, with a trial or a new deal ahead. It wouldn’t touch the state murder conviction either.

Every card comes from the court record, or from a broadcast or a report that says what the record doesn’t. The cards from 2024 on rely on reporting, because the trial court hasn’t posted the later petitions or its orders on them.
The evening at 38th Street and Chicago Avenue, as the courts later described it.
A call about a fake $20 bill

Just after 8 p.m. a clerk at Cup Foods calls 911 about a customer who paid with a counterfeit bill. Officers Thomas Lane and J. Alexander Kueng find George Floyd in a car across the street. Lane drew his gun at the driver’s window and yelled at Floyd to put his hands up. Floyd, crying, told him several times, “Please don’t shoot me.” The officers handcuffed him and walked him to their squad car, where he resisted getting in and said he was claustrophobic. A struggle followed at the car, and two more officers, Derek Chauvin and Tou Thao, arrived to help. The caller had told 911 that Floyd seemed to be under the influence of something, and two passengers had been in the car with him. Ct. App. opinion, Apr 17, 2023 pp. 3–4 · Order of Oct 21, 2020 pp. 16–20

At 8:19 p.m. the officers put Floyd on the pavement, handcuffed and face down. Chauvin presses his left knee into his neck and keeps it there until the ambulance crew is ready to move him. Floyd said again and again that he couldn’t breathe. About four minutes and 45 seconds in he went silent, and 53 seconds after that he stopped responding. An off-duty firefighter offered to help and was turned away. At 8:25 Kueng said he couldn’t find a pulse. Chauvin answered “huh” and kept his knee where it was. The appeals court put the whole restraint at about nine minutes and 29 seconds. A crowd on the sidewalk shouted at the officers to check his pulse and get off him, and a 17-year-old, Darnella Frazier, filmed it on her phone. Her video was seen around the world. Ct. App. opinion pp. 4–5 · Order of Oct 21, 2020 pp. 22–29 · Star Tribune, day-by-day recap

At 9:25 p.m. at Hennepin County Medical Center. The county’s medical examiner later rules the death a homicide. Dr. Andrew Baker gave the cause as “cardiopulmonary arrest complicating law enforcement subdual, restraint, and neck compression.” He listed heart disease, fentanyl and recent methamphetamine use as other significant conditions. His office noted that “homicide” on a death record is a medical finding, not a legal one about blame or intent. Those other conditions are where the defense would build its case about how Floyd died. Order of Oct 21, 2020 p. 29 · Autopsy report pp. 12–24
Four days later, the first charges. Three days after that, a bigger one.

The Hennepin County Attorney charges Chauvin with third-degree murder and second-degree manslaughter. The complaint quoted the medical examiner’s first findings, that the autopsy showed “no physical findings that support a diagnosis of traumatic asphyxia or strangulation,” and that the restraint, heart disease and “any potential intoxicants” likely combined. The defense would quote that line for months. No grand jury was used. In Minnesota a complaint is how most crimes are charged. Chauvin’s third petition, filed in 2026, says that was a mistake in a case like his. Complaint, May 29, 2020 p. 3

Gov. Tim Walz puts the state’s Attorney General, Keith Ellison, in charge of the prosecution. Until then it had been the case of the Hennepin County Attorney, Mike Freeman. Floyd’s family had asked for Ellison to take it over. This is the step Chauvin’s third petition, filed in August 2026, calls illegitimate. WCCO, May 31, 2020 · MPR News, Aug 18, 2026

An amended complaint adds the charge he’d be convicted of. The other three officers are charged too, with aiding and abetting. That made three counts. The new one, second-degree unintentional murder, means causing a death without meaning to while committing a felony, and the felony here was third-degree assault. The other two were third-degree murder and second-degree manslaughter. The complaint said his knee was on Floyd’s neck for “8 minutes and 46 seconds in total.” That number changed once the videos were studied. At trial the State’s figure was nine minutes and 29 seconds. Amended complaint pp. 1–2, 4
A dropped charge, a televised trial ordered, and a fight over whether to bring the charge back.
He asks the court to dismiss the charges

His lawyer, Eric Nelson, says there isn’t probable cause for any of them, and asks to move the trial out of Minneapolis. The defense memo said Floyd “most likely died from an opioid overdose,” and quoted notes of the medical examiner telling prosecutors an overdose label would have been “acceptable” if Floyd had been found dead at home with no other apparent cause. Nelson also asked the court to take the Hennepin County Attorney’s office off the case over its meeting with the medical examiner. The same day, the State gave notice that it would ask for a sentence longer than the guidelines allow. Defense memorandum, Aug 28, 2020 p. 22 · State’s notice, Aug 28, 2020

He leaves prison to wait for trial at home. He’d been held since the day he was charged. He would stay free until the verdicts were read, when the judge sent him back into custody on the spot. Notice of release, Oct 7, 2020 · Federal judgment p. 2

Judge Peter Cahill dismisses the third-degree murder count for lack of probable cause. Second-degree murder and manslaughter stay. Minnesota’s depraved-mind murder law covers acts “eminently dangerous to others,” and the judge read that as excluding acts aimed only at the person who died. Nothing showed Chauvin’s acts endangered anyone but Floyd, he found. His 107-page order sets out the evening minute by minute from the body cameras, and many of the times on these pages come from it. It was written at an early stage, where a court takes the facts in the light most favorable to the prosecution. Order of Oct 21, 2020 p. 2, 54–60

The judge lets the trial be televised and orders an anonymous jury. For now, all four officers will be tried together, in Minneapolis. The State didn’t consent to cameras. All four defendants asked for them. The rules the country watched under came from this order: up to three fixed cameras, no juror ever on screen, and no witness under 18 shown without written consent. The judge kept the trial in Hennepin County, finding that “no corner of the [s]tate of Minnesota has been shielded from pretrial publicity,” and said he’d look at it again if things changed. Camera order pp. 2–4 · Venue order, Nov 4, 2020 · Juror order, Nov 4, 2020 · Joinder order, Nov 4, 2020 · Ct. App. opinion p. 6
His trial is split from the other three

Not even the building’s largest courtroom, C-1856, can hold four defendants and their lawyers six feet apart, the judge finds. He severs Chauvin’s case, and Chauvin will be tried alone, starting March 8. The judge turned down the State’s request to put everything off to June because of the pandemic. The other three officers’ trial was moved to August 2021. Order of Jan 11, 2021 pp. 3–4
The judge won’t bring back third-degree murder

Ten days earlier the appeals court upheld a depraved-mind murder conviction in another Minneapolis police case. The State asks to restore the count. The judge says that decision isn’t final yet. The other case was Mohamed Noor’s, an officer who shot a woman who had called 911. On February 1, 2021, the Court of Appeals held that third-degree murder can rest on an act aimed at one person. The State appealed the judge’s refusal to follow it. Order of Feb 11, 2021
The appeals court says to follow Noor

Jury selection, then three weeks of evidence in a courtroom rebuilt for distancing, on television from start to finish.

One possible juror at a time, questioned by the judge and then by each side. Each had filled out a long questionnaire months before. For jury selection the judge gave the defense 18 peremptory strikes and the State 10, more than the usual five and three. The questionnaire asked what each person had seen of the video and the protests, about Black Lives Matter and Blue Lives Matter, and about police reform. Jurors were known only by number. No camera ever showed one. Ct. App. opinion pp. 7, 17 · Trial management order

With jury selection already under way, the judge restores the count. The jury will decide three charges. Later in 2021 the Minnesota Supreme Court reversed Noor’s conviction and held that depraved-mind murder can’t rest on conduct aimed at one person. By then Chauvin had been convicted only of second-degree murder, so his third-degree verdict was never entered, and the appeals court declined to rule on it. Order of Mar 13, 2021 p. 2 · Ct. App. opinion p. 24

Minneapolis settles the Floyd family’s wrongful-death lawsuit, in the middle of jury selection. Three days later Chauvin asked for a change of venue, a continuance or a jury locked away from the news. The judge called back the seven jurors already seated and questioned them about the settlement, and excused two for cause. The rest of his requests were turned down. Ct. App. opinion pp. 8–9

Twelve to decide the case, two alternates, and a fifteenth to be let go if everyone else stayed. The defense finished with three of its strikes unused. The fifteenth juror was released before opening statements, and the two alternates were told who they were only after closing arguments. NPR, Apr 20, 2021 · Ct. App. opinion p. 17

In both arrests, the judge wrote, Floyd put drugs in his mouth as police approached, and after being handcuffed he “complains of problems breathing and calls out for his mother.” None of the four officers had been there in 2019. The jury could weigh it only on what drugs may have done to Floyd’s body. It was “not to be used as evidence of the character of George Floyd,” the judge told them. “The most important numbers you will hear in this trial are 9:29”

Jerry Blackwell opens for the State. Chauvin “betrayed this badge,” he says, when he used excessive force on a man who was handcuffed and defenseless. Blackwell told the jury it would hear Floyd say “I can’t breathe” 27 times in the first four minutes and 45 seconds, and see him go still. The State’s first witnesses were the 911 dispatcher who watched on a city camera and called a sergeant, a store clerk who filmed, and Donald Williams, a mixed martial arts fighter who called the hold a “blood choke.” Tr. “The evidence is far greater than nine minutes and 29 seconds”

Chauvin “did exactly what he had been trained to do over the course of his 19 year career,” Nelson said. Three officers couldn’t get Floyd into the squad car, and a growing, angry crowd was seen as a threat. On the cause of death, he said the evidence would show a heart rhythm problem brought on by heart disease, with fentanyl and methamphetamine, and none of the “telltale signs of asphyxiation.” Tr. A nine-year-old who was with her testified too, and Nelson didn’t question her. Genevieve Hansen, the firefighter, said, “There is a man being killed, and I would have been able to provide medical attention.” Nelson’s questions to the bystanders were about the crowd getting louder and angrier. Chief Medaria Arradondo tells the jury that once Floyd stopped resisting, and certainly once he was in distress, the force should have ended. That day and the next, the department’s own trainers said a knee on the neck of a handcuffed man isn’t what they teach, and that officers are trained to roll a person into the recovery position. Shown a photo of the hold, the former head of training, Katie Blackwell, said, “I don’t know what kind of improvised position this is.” Chauvin’s 2025 petition says those officers misdescribed the training. The State’s doctors: he died from a lack of oxygen

A lung specialist, an emergency physician and a retired medical examiner say the restraint, not drugs or heart disease, caused his death. A toxicologist says the drugs in his blood don’t look like an overdose. Dr. Martin Tobin, a pulmonologist, walked the jury through the video and said Floyd “died from a low level of oxygen.” Dr. Bill Smock said, “That is not a fentanyl overdose. That is someone begging to breathe.” Dr. Andrew Baker, who did the autopsy, stood by his finding of homicide and said the restraint and the neck compression were “just more than Mr. Floyd could take by virtue of those heart conditions.” On April 12 a cardiologist, Dr. Jonathan Rich, called the death “absolutely preventable.” Tr. A police shooting in the suburb of Brooklyn Center sets off protests and unrest. The defense asks to sequester the jury, and the judge says no. The jurors were already partly sequestered, brought in and out of the building by deputies and kept apart from everyone else in it. The judge told them again to stay away from any news of the case. A use-of-force expert, Barry Brodd, says Chauvin was justified. A retired medical examiner, Dr. David Fowler, says heart disease, drugs and other factors together caused the death. Brodd, a retired police officer, said Chauvin was “acting with objective reasonableness,” and didn’t count holding Floyd face down as force at all. Fowler, a former chief medical examiner of Maryland, said Floyd’s heart went into a fatal rhythm during the restraint and didn’t list a lack of oxygen as a cause. Shawanda Hill, who was in the car, said Floyd had fallen asleep before the police came. Another passenger, Morries Hall, had said he’d take the Fifth if called, and he wasn’t called. Tr. Brodd · Tr. Hill · Notice of Mar 31, 2021 · Star Tribune, day-by-day recap

With the jury out of the room, Chauvin tells the judge he’ll use his Fifth Amendment right. The defense rests. He told the judge it was his decision alone. A juror said in an interview after the verdict that the jurors had talked about it anyway, which became part of his appeal. AP, Apr 15, 2021 · Ct. App. opinion p. 10

Steve Schleicher closes for the State: “Believe your eyes.” Jerry Blackwell gets the last word. Floyd died, he says, “because Mr. Chauvin’s heart was too small.” Schleicher told the jury the case was “not called the State of Minnesota v. The Police,” and called it “a pro-police prosecution.” Of the claim that Floyd died of an overdose, he said, “That’s not common sense. That’s nonsense.” Tr. Closing, 01:42:51 · 14:10 · 43:05 · NPR, Apr 19, 2021

On the cause of death: “If a person has drugs in their system and that drug causes an overdose in the context of the police restraint, it’s not the natural consequence of the restraint. It’s the natural consequence of the deceased’s actions.” Tr. Defense closing, 54:53 · NPR, Apr 19, 2021

Before the jury goes out, Nelson asks for a mistrial over the publicity and a congresswoman’s words. The judge says no, and the jury begins to deliberate. Rep. Maxine Waters of California had said that if Chauvin were acquitted, protesters should “stay on the street” and “get more confrontational.” Ct. App. opinion p. 9

The jury finds him guilty of second-degree murder, third-degree murder and second-degree manslaughter. It had agreed by 1:45 p.m. on its second day. Judge Cahill read the verdicts that afternoon and then asked each juror, by number, if they were theirs. All twelve said yes. The foreperson was Juror 19. The State asked for his bail to be revoked, and the judge did it on the spot and sent him into the sheriff’s custody. Verdict, Count I · Count II · Count III · Tr. Verdict
The state sentence, then a federal case of its own, over the same evening and one other.

A federal grand jury’s indictment charges all four officers with violating Floyd’s constitutional rights. A second one charges Chauvin over a 2017 arrest of a 14-year-old boy. The federal crime is using the power of a police job, under color of law, to take away someone’s rights, here the right to be free from unreasonable force. A state and the federal government can each prosecute the same act, because they’re separate governments. In the 2017 case, by his own later admission, he hit the boy in the head with a flashlight, held him by the throat, and knelt on his neck and back for 15 to 16 minutes while he lay handcuffed and not resisting. Indictment, ECF 1 · Plea agreement pp. 6–7
Four reasons for a longer sentence

Chauvin had given up a jury on this, so the judge decides: he abused his position of trust and authority, treated Floyd with particular cruelty, did it in front of children, and acted with three others. “It was particularly cruel to kill George Floyd slowly by preventing his ability to breathe when Mr. Floyd had already made it clear he was having trouble breathing,” the judge wrote. He found the State hadn’t proved a fifth reason it had argued, that Floyd was particularly vulnerable. Findings of May 11, 2021 pp. 3–5 · Sentencing order p. 4

That’s double the top of the guidelines range for someone with no criminal record. The presumptive sentence for second-degree unintentional murder, with no record, is 150 months, inside a range of 128 to 180. The State asked for 360 months. State’s memorandum, Jun 2, 2021

His lawyer asks for time served and probation, saying that in his mind Chauvin was “simply performing his lawful duty.” The memo called what he did “an error made in good faith reliance” on his experience and training, “not intentional commission of an illegal act.” He had also asked for a new trial, on 11 grounds, from the publicity to a juror’s answers in jury selection. Defense memorandum, Jun 2, 2021 p. 11

The judge turns down a new trial, and a hearing to question jurors about misconduct. He found Chauvin hadn’t shown that the court “abused its discretion or committed error such that Defendant was deprived of his constitutional right to a fair trial,” or any misconduct by the prosecutors or the jurors. Order of Jun 24, 2021

Twenty-two and a half years, ten years past the presumptive sentence. He’s convicted of second-degree murder. The other two guilty verdicts are never entered, because they’re lesser offenses of it. The judge rested the sentence on two of the four reasons, the abuse of trust and the particular cruelty. A sentence can’t rest on “sympathy, bias, passion, or public opinion,” he wrote, and Chauvin “treated Mr. Floyd without respect and denied him the dignity owed to all human beings.” Before the sentence, Chauvin offered his condolences to Floyd’s family and said, “There’s going to be some other information in the future that would be of interest.” His mother spoke for him, and two of Floyd’s brothers spoke in court. Sentencing order pp. 1–2, 20–22 · NPR, Jun 25, 2021

In federal court in St. Paul, Chauvin pleads guilty to violating Floyd’s rights, and to the 2017 count. In his plea agreement he admitted that “no later than the time the officers decided not to apply the hobble,” his force “became objectively unreasonable and excessive,” and that he knew it was wrong “in part, because it was contrary to his training.” He agreed that his actions kept Floyd from getting enough oxygen to live. The deal called for 20 to 25 years, served at the same time as his state sentence, in federal prison. The 2017 count came in by information, and the separate 2017 indictment was dropped. Plea transcript p. 22 · Plea agreement pp. 1–6
The other three officers are convicted in federal court

A federal jury finds Tou Thao, J. Alexander Kueng and Thomas Lane guilty of violating Floyd’s rights. Chauvin, having pleaded, wasn’t part of that trial. All three were convicted of depriving Floyd of medical care, and Thao and Kueng also of failing to stop Chauvin. Their cases are separate from this one. AP, Feb 24, 2022

Judge Paul Magnuson sentences him to 252 months, cut to 245, running at the same time as his state sentence. That’s 240 months for violating Floyd’s rights and 12 for the 2017 count, then five years of supervised release. The 245 months make up for time he spent in state custody that federal prison won’t count. The government had asked for 25 years. Judgment pp. 2–3 · Government memorandum, ECF 375
Twelve reasons the verdict and the sentence were wrong, and three courts that wouldn’t change either.

His new lawyer, William Mohrman, files his brief in the Court of Appeals. The biggest arguments are the publicity, a juror, and whether a police officer can commit felony murder at all. He argued the trial should have been moved or delayed, pointing to the riots, the settlement and a courthouse “surrounded by barbed wire and soldiers.” And he said the felony-murder law turns into “strict liability” for police, because officers are “duty bound to ‘assault’ suspects resisting arrest.” His appeal brief p. 57, 65

Its brief, written with the lawyer Neal Katyal, calls the appeal “an industrial kitchen-sink’s worth of arguments.” “George Floyd did not die because of a heart attack, drugs, carbon monoxide, or a tumor, as the defense alternatively tried to claim,” it said. “George Floyd died for a simple reason: because he could not breathe.” Chauvin “says the quiet part out loud,” it said, “and argues that police officers cannot ever be convicted of assault.” State’s appeal brief pp. 19–21
Argued in the Court of Appeals

Before three judges, at 9:30 in the morning, and streamed live. The panel was Judges Reyes, Larson and Klaphake, the last a retired judge serving by appointment. Judge Reyes wrote the opinion. Ct. App. opinion p. 1 · Minnesota Judicial Branch

All twelve arguments fail. A police officer who uses unreasonable force that amounts to assault can be convicted of felony murder, the court holds. “Police officers undoubtedly have a challenging, difficult, and sometimes dangerous job,” the court wrote. “However, no one is above the law.” On the publicity, it held that refusing to move or delay a trial is no mistake when a judge takes enough steps to make sure the jurors can be fair. On the sentence, it held that the particular cruelty alone justified going past the guidelines. Ct. App. opinion, Apr 17, 2023 pp. 1–2, 48–50
The Minnesota Supreme Court won’t hear it

It turns down his petition for review, ending his direct appeal in the state courts. Turning a case down isn’t a ruling on it. It leaves the Court of Appeals’ decision as the last word. Docket, No. 23-416
His federal appeal is too late

He’d filed it himself, a year after his federal sentence. The Eighth Circuit dismisses it as untimely. His plea deal had already given up his right to appeal anything but the court’s power over the case. His lawyer, Eric Nelson, withdrew from the federal case that September. Eighth Circuit, ECF 538 · Government response p. 3 · ECF 541
The U.S. Supreme Court won’t hear it either

It turns down his petition for certiorari. Minnesota hadn’t even filed a response. He asked the Court whether a community that had lived through “catastrophic violent riots” should be presumed biased against a police officer, and whether evidence after a trial that a juror hid his views has to be considered. The Minneapolis police officers’ union filed a brief supporting him. Petition p. 2 · Docket, No. 23-416
Since 2023 he has gone back to both courts, with new lawyers and new theories. Nothing has been undone.
He asks to undo his federal guilty plea

Filing on his own, he says his lawyer never told him a pathologist had written that a tumor, not Chauvin, caused Floyd’s death. The pathologist, Dr. William Schaetzel, had emailed Nelson, the judge’s chambers and a county prosecutor during the 2021 trial about the tumor the autopsy found. Chauvin says that if he’d known, he “would not have pled guilty.” His plea deal had given up this kind of motion except for ineffective assistance of counsel, which is the claim he makes. The government answered that the autopsy findings “came out at his state trial,” and that the same kind of expert testimony “was not persuasive to the jury.” Motion to vacate, ECF 544 · Schaetzel email p. 11 · Government response pp. 7, 11

Another prisoner stabs him 22 times at the federal prison in Tucson, Arizona. He survives, and the man is charged with attempted murder. The man told investigators he targeted Chauvin because of the case. In 2024 Chauvin was moved to a low-security federal prison in Big Spring, Texas. AP, Aug 20, 2024
His first petition in state court

A post-conviction petition, the way to challenge a state conviction once the appeal is over. It centered on the tumor found at the autopsy, and on whether the medical examiner had been pushed toward calling the death a homicide. Chauvin later said he didn’t mean to argue those points there. Star Tribune, Dec 4, 2025

In the federal case, Judge Magnuson lets the defense examine tissue samples, slides, fluids and photographs from the autopsy. The government asked him to reconsider. He refused, reminding it that “this matter is separate from Defendant’s state prosecution.” In January 2025 he put the hearing off for up to 90 days while the testing went on, and asked for a report every 30 days. Judge Paul Scoggin of the district court notes that many of its points were argued at trial, and that Chauvin can file again. The judge also noted that Chauvin was challenging his federal sentence at the same time. Star Tribune, Dec 4, 2025

He argues the State’s doctors drew conclusions from video instead of medical findings, that the police chief and two trainers misdescribed the department’s training, backed by statements from 57 current and former officers, and that the jury instructions were flawed. The court, he wrote, was now “removed from the hysteria of the day and can finally look at the facts and evidence through a clear lens.” Star Tribune, Dec 4, 2025

He appeals the denial. It’s the second time his state case has gone up. The appeal is pending. Fox News, Jul 9, 2026 · MPR News, Jul 1, 2026

Where it lands The jury said the force wasn’t authorized, and his own federal plea says it became unreasonable.
Can a police officer commit felony murder by using force in an arrest?

Prosecution Yes, when the force is unreasonable. The law only allows reasonable force, so force beyond that is an assault like anyone else’s, and a death caused by it is murder. He “says the quiet part out loud” by arguing officers can never be convicted of assault. Defense No. Officers are “duty bound to ‘assault’ suspects resisting arrest,” so using assault as the felony turns murder into a crime of “strict liability” for police, with no need to prove any intent to harm. Court Yes. The Court of Appeals held that an officer can be convicted of second-degree felony murder for a death caused by unreasonable force that amounts to third-degree assault. The decision is binding law in Minnesota. State’s appeal brief p. 20 · His appeal brief p. 65 · Ct. App. opinion p. 2 Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Prosecution The argument Felony murder here needs an assault, and an assault needs only the intent to use the force, not to cause the harm it causes. An officer who uses force the law allows commits no assault. An officer who uses force past what the law allows does, and the jury found he did. Rests on The statute allowing officers reasonable force, and the jury’s finding that his wasn’t. State’s appeal brief p. 20 · Ct. App. opinion pp. 26–27 Authority Minnesota’s assault and felony-murder laws, and the Minnesota Supreme Court’s ruling that assault of this kind is a general-intent crime. Where it is weak It means an officer can be convicted of murder without having meant to hurt anyone, which is the point the defense pressed. Defense The argument Every arrest involves force an officer means to use, so every officer intends the physical act. If that’s enough for assault, and assault is enough for murder, an officer whose arrest ends in a death can be convicted without the State proving he meant any injury. The legislature didn’t mean that, and strict-liability crimes are disfavored. Rests on The jury instruction that the State didn’t have to prove he meant to cause substantial bodily harm. His appeal brief pp. 65–66 · Jury instructions pp. 5–6 Authority Cases holding that crimes without a guilty mind are disfavored, and Graham v. Connor. Where it is weak His argument depends on officers being allowed whatever force they use. The law allows only reasonable force, and the court said that’s what keeps the crime from being strict liability. Ct. App. opinion pp. 26–27 Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Is unreasonable force by an officer an assault that can carry a felony-murder charge? Defense Officers must use force, so this makes them guilty without any intent. The intent Only the force has to be intended, as for anyone. The intent That turns murder into strict liability for police. Prosecution The law allows reasonable force only. Past that, an officer is like anyone else. Where it lands Decided. An officer can be convicted when the force is unreasonable. It’s now the law in Minnesota.
Could he get a fair trial in Minneapolis?

Prosecution Yes. This case was going to draw enormous publicity wherever and whenever it was tried, and the court did everything it could to seat a fair jury. Every juror who served said they could decide on the evidence. Defense No. The riots, the city’s $27 million settlement during jury selection, a courthouse “surrounded by barbed wire and soldiers,” and a congresswoman’s call to “get more confrontational” put jurors in fear of the result. The trial should have been moved, delayed or the jury locked away. Court No mistake. Denying those requests is fine when the judge takes enough steps and checks that the jurors can be fair, the Court of Appeals held, and Judge Cahill did. State’s appeal brief pp. 19–20 · His appeal brief p. 57 · Ct. App. opinion pp. 14–20 Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Prosecution The argument Moving the trial wouldn’t have helped, because no corner of the state had escaped the publicity, and waiting wouldn’t have either. What protects a defendant is the care taken in picking the jury, and here it was extraordinary. Rests on A long questionnaire sent months ahead. Jurors questioned one at a time. Extra strikes for the defense, 18 against 10. Jurors removed for cause the moment the settlement changed their view. The two seated jurors excused over it. Ct. App. opinion pp. 16–17 · Venue order, Nov 4, 2020 Authority The U.S. Supreme Court in Skilling v. United States (2010), that “prominence does not necessarily produce prejudice,” and the Minnesota Supreme Court’s State v. Blom (2004). Where it is weak The building was fortified, the city settled in the middle of selection, and one seated juror said her safety “really depends on how the trial” ends. His appeal brief p. 58 · Ct. App. opinion p. 8 Defense The argument This is one of the rare cases where the atmosphere was so charged that prejudice should be presumed, without having to prove what any one juror thought. Jurors walked past soldiers and razor wire every day. A wrong verdict, as they’d have understood it, would have had consequences for the Twin Cities. Rests on The security around the courthouse, the National Guard, businesses boarded up, the settlement, officials calling the death a murder, and a leak about a failed plea deal before jury selection. His appeal brief pp. 57–60 · Ct. App. opinion p. 9 Authority Sheppard v. Maxwell (1966), Rideau v. Louisiana (1963) and Irvin v. Dowd (1961), the U.S. Supreme Court’s cases on trials overwhelmed by publicity. Where it is weak He finished jury selection with three strikes unused, which courts read as a sign a defendant accepted the jury, and every juror said they could be fair. Ct. App. opinion p. 17 Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Did the court do enough to make sure these jurors could set aside what they’d heard? Defense The atmosphere was so charged that prejudice should be presumed. The jury Questioned one by one, with extra strikes and removals. The jury Walked past soldiers every day, afraid of the result. Prosecution Moving or waiting wouldn’t have helped. Careful selection did. Where it lands Decided. The court took enough steps, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to look again.
Did a juror hide views that should have kept him off the jury?

Prosecution No. Juror 52 answered the questionnaire truthfully. What he said in interviews afterward doesn’t show he lied in jury selection. Defense Yes. He didn’t mention going to a march in Washington in August 2020 where Floyd’s family spoke, and after the trial he said he’d been pulled over by Minneapolis police “probably about 50 times” and saw a “chance to make history.” The court should at least have held a hearing. Court No hearing was needed. The court found he answered truthfully, and that the other juror Chauvin named was an alternate who never deliberated. Ct. App. opinion p. 10 · 20–23 · His appeal brief pp. 60–63 Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Prosecution The argument The questionnaire asked specific questions, and his answers to them were accurate. A juror isn’t dishonest for not volunteering things nobody asked about, and he said in selection that he could be fair. Rests on His questionnaire and his answers in jury selection. Ct. App. opinion pp. 21–23 Authority The Minnesota rule that a hearing on juror misconduct needs a real showing of misconduct first. Where it is weak His words after the trial were never tested under oath, because no hearing was held. Defense The argument A juror who hid strong views about the Minneapolis police and took part in a protest about Floyd’s death couldn’t be impartial, and the only way to find out what he concealed was to question him under oath. Rests on The juror’s interviews after the verdict, and the march he hadn’t mentioned. Ct. App. opinion p. 10 Authority Schwartz v. Minneapolis Suburban Bus Co. (1960), which set up the hearing, and the right to an impartial jury. Where it is weak He didn’t fully argue part of it in his brief, the court said, and he had three strikes left he could have used during selection. Ct. App. opinion pp. 20–23 Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Was there enough sign of misconduct to put the juror back under oath? Defense His interviews show views he kept back in selection. His answers True to what the questionnaire asked. His answers Silent about the march and the 50 stops. Prosecution Nothing he said afterward shows a false answer. Where it lands Decided. No hearing, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to take the question.
Was 22 and a half years the right sentence?

Prosecution It should have been 30. He abused the trust of his badge, killed Floyd slowly and cruelly in front of children, and did it with three other officers. Defense It should have been probation, or at least a shorter term. In his mind he was “simply performing his lawful duty,” relying in good faith on his training, and a police officer’s authority had nothing to do with Floyd. Court Judge Cahill found four aggravating factors and relied on two, the abuse of trust and the particular cruelty, for 270 months. The Court of Appeals upheld it on the cruelty alone. State’s memorandum, Jun 2, 2021 · Defense memorandum p. 11 · Sentencing order p. 4 · Ct. App. opinion p. 48 Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Prosecution The argument This was worse than a typical case of the crime in every way the guidelines count. Floyd begged for his life and was ignored, he was killed slowly, children watched, and an officer used the authority of his job to do it. That justifies doubling the top of the range, to 360 months. Rests on The trial evidence and the judge’s findings of four aggravating factors. State’s memorandum, Jun 2, 2021 · Findings of May 11, 2021 pp. 3–5 Authority The Minnesota Sentencing Guidelines’ list of aggravating factors, which includes particular cruelty. Where it is weak No Minnesota case had applied “abuse of a position of trust” to a police officer, and the appeals court didn’t rely on it. Ct. App. opinion p. 48 Defense The argument He had no criminal record, he was compliant on release, and he didn’t set out to commit a crime. His error was made “in good faith reliance” on his experience and training. An abuse of authority over Floyd doesn’t fit, because he didn’t put the handcuffs on him. Rests on His record, his conduct out on bond, and the training evidence. Defense memorandum p. 11 · His appeal brief pp. 67–70 Authority The guidelines’ rule that a departure needs “substantial and compelling” reasons, which he said the court didn’t have. Where it is weak The judge found the cruelty proved beyond a reasonable doubt, and the average sentence in Minnesota for the same crime with an aggravating factor and no record was 278.2 months, longer than his. Sentencing order p. 21 · Ct. App. opinion p. 49 Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Was this crime significantly worse than the usual one of its kind? Prosecution Cruel, slow, in front of children, and by an officer using his badge. The factors Four proved, two enough. The factors An officer’s authority had nothing to do with Floyd. Defense An error made in good faith deserves probation or less. Where it lands 270 months, upheld. Cruelty alone carries it.
Should the state case be reopened now?

Prosecution Its answers to the petitions aren’t public. On the same points at trial and on appeal it said the medical experts were sound, the officers’ testimony about training was true, and the jury instructions were correct, and the courts agreed. Defense Yes. The State’s doctors testified from video, not medical findings. The police chief and two trainers misdescribed the training, and 57 officers say so. And the whole case was structurally flawed, handed to the wrong prosecutor and charged without a grand jury. Court The second petition was denied on May 1, 2026: “None of the claims raised in this Petition for Post-Conviction Relief warrant relief.” Its appeal and the third petition are undecided. Star Tribune, Dec 4, 2025 · MPR News, Aug 18, 2026 · Fox News, Jul 9, 2026 Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Prosecution The argument Its 2026 answers aren’t public. At trial and on appeal it defended each point now raised: the doctors’ testimony, the officers’ account of the training, and the jury instructions, which the appeals court found had no plain error. Rests on The trial record and the 2023 appeal. State’s appeal brief pp. 19–21 · Ct. App. opinion pp. 27–33 Authority The Knaffla rule, which keeps a petition from arguing again what was or could have been argued on appeal, and the judge applied it throughout. Where it is weak The officers’ statements about what was really trained, and the experts he now offers, haven’t been tested in a hearing. Defense The argument The trial was a product of its moment. A court “removed from the hysteria of the day” can now see that the doctors read video instead of doing medicine, that officials testified falsely about training and nobody corrected it, and that the Attorney General had no lawful power to prosecute at all, so the conviction can’t stand. Rests on Affidavits from 57 current and former officers, a judge’s ruling in a separate defamation case that the department’s materials showed similar techniques, and outside forensic experts. Star Tribune, Dec 4, 2025 · MPR News, Aug 18, 2026 Authority The right to due process, and the rule that structural errors can’t be waived. He calls the governor’s order handing the case to the Attorney General “illegitimate.” Where it is weak The judge found most of the 2025 claims were or could have been raised on appeal. And Minnesota’s rules require a grand jury only for crimes that carry life in prison, which second-degree murder doesn’t. Fox News, Jul 9, 2026 · Minn. R. Crim. P. 17.01 Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Is there something new, or so basic it wasn’t waived, that undoes a final conviction? Defense The experts, the training testimony and the charging were all wrong. What’s new Nothing. It was argued, or could have been, before. What’s new 57 officers’ statements, and a flaw in the charge itself. Prosecution Its answers aren’t public. The judge applied Knaffla. Where it lands One petition denied and on appeal, one pending.
Should his federal guilty plea be undone?

Prosecution No. He pleaded knowingly after a careful hearing, waived this kind of challenge, and admitted his actions kept Floyd from getting enough oxygen. The autopsy findings were aired at his state trial, and the same kind of testimony “was not persuasive to the jury.” Defense Yes. His lawyer never told him that a pathologist had concluded the tumor found at the autopsy, not Chauvin, caused Floyd’s death. Had he known, he “would not have pled guilty, and would have insisted on going to trial.” Court Undecided. The judge let his experts examine Floyd’s heart tissue and fluids, finding they “could support” the pathologist’s opinion, and has put the hearing off since January 2025 while the testing goes on. Government response pp. 7, 11 · Motion to vacate p. 2 · Order, ECF 565 p. 3 Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Prosecution The argument His plea waived every later challenge except a claim that his lawyer failed him, and that claim fails. He told the judge under questioning that he understood what he was giving up. A lawyer isn’t ineffective for not passing on a theory the jury in his state trial had already heard and rejected. Rests on The plea agreement, the plea hearing transcript, and the state trial record. Government response pp. 3–4 · Plea transcript p. 22 Authority The waiver in his plea agreement, and the U.S. Supreme Court’s test for a lawyer’s failure, Strickland v. Washington (1984). Where it is weak The judge found good cause to let the testing go ahead over the government’s objection, and reminded it that “this matter is separate from Defendant’s state prosecution.” Order, ECF 565 p. 3 · Order, ECF 567 Defense The argument A pathologist, Dr. William Schaetzel, wrote during the state trial that Floyd’s tumor released a surge of adrenaline-like hormones that led to heart failure. His lawyer had that and kept it from him while advising him to take the deal. That’s ineffective assistance, and it made his plea unknowing. Rests on Dr. Schaetzel’s email of April 2021, a second doctor’s report, and the autopsy’s description of the tumor. Motion to vacate, ECF 544 · Schaetzel email p. 11 · Reply, ECF 562 Authority Strickland v. Washington, and Hill v. Lockhart (1985), which applies it to guilty pleas. Where it is weak He admitted in his plea agreement that his actions impaired Floyd’s ability to get enough oxygen, and that his force became unreasonable. The medical examiner called the tumor incidental. Plea agreement pp. 4–6 · Autopsy report p. 24 Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Did his lawyer fall short, and would he have gone to trial if he hadn’t? Defense He’d never have pleaded if he’d known about the tumor theory. The theory Already heard at the state trial, and rejected. The theory Never tested, until the tissue is examined. Prosecution He pleaded knowingly and admitted the facts. Where it lands Undecided. Testing allowed in December 2024, and nothing public since.
